blogs.title: Fibroids or Ovaries? Navigating Abdominal Mass Imaging in Pregnancy
blogs.description: This post explores the diagnostic dilemma of distinguishing uterine leiomyomas from adnexal masses (like endometriomas) during pregnancy. We discuss the limitations of ultrasound in the gravid uterus, the safety and superior anatomical definition of non-contrast MRI, and how imaging characteristics (solid vs. cystic, continuity with uterus) guide the differential diagnosis.

blogs.title: The CA-125 Trap: Interpreting Tumor Markers in the Pregnant Patient
blogs.description: Elevated CA-125 often triggers alarm for ovarian malignancy, but pregnancy alters the baseline. This blog breaks down the physiologic peaks of CA-125 across trimesters, the significance of trends versus isolated values, and why benign conditions like myomas or endometriosis can mimic malignancy in the second trimester.

blogs.title: When to Cut: Indications for Non-Obstetric Surgery in the Second Trimester
blogs.description: Expectant management is standard for pelvic masses in pregnancy, but when is surgery mandatory? We analyze the risk-benefit ratio of operating during the second trimester, focusing on indications such as intractable pain, dyspnea from mass effect, and signs of torsion or necrosis, while weighing the risks of preterm labor.

blogs.title: Protecting the Pregnancy: Perioperative Safety During Myomectomy
blogs.description: Once the decision to operate is made, how do we minimize obstetric risk? This post details intraoperative protocols including continuous fetal heart rate monitoring, the use of progesterone prophylaxis to maintain the pregnancy, and surgical techniques to reduce operative time and bleeding.

blogs.title: The Final Mile: How Pelvic Masses Dictate Mode of Delivery
blogs.description: Not all masses are removed during pregnancy. This blog discusses the long-term management of residual pelvic fibroids, specifically how their location and size impact the expulsive phase of labor, and the criteria for planning an elective cesarean section versus attempting a vaginal delivery.
